input: The city council of Millbrook voted 6-3 on Tuesday to approve a $42 million plan to replace the aging Harbor Street bridge, which has been rated structurally deficient since 2019. Construction is expected to begin in March and last 22 months, during which a temporary pedestrian crossing will remain open. Drivers will be detoured through Pine Avenue, and the city says it will add two bus routes to offset the delay. Council member Dana Ortiz, who voted against the plan, argued that the cost was too high and that a cheaper repair would have bought ten more years. The mayor said federal grants will cover 60 percent of the cost.

Researchers at a university lab reported that a new battery design using sodium instead of lithium retained 90 percent of its capacity after 2,000 charge cycles. Sodium is far more abundant and cheaper than lithium, but sodium batteries have historically stored less energy per kilogram. The team said their prototype stores about 160 watt-hours per kilogram, roughly two thirds of a typical lithium-ion cell. They believe the technology is best suited to grid storage rather than phones or cars. The results have not yet been peer reviewed, and the lab is seeking an industry partner to test larger cells.

A regional airline cancelled 140 flights over the weekend after a software failure disrupted its crew scheduling system. About 18,000 passengers were affected, and many were stranded overnight at hub airports. The airline said it restored the system by Sunday evening and will offer rebooking and meal vouchers, but it did not say whether it would pay cash compensation. A passenger advocacy group criticized the company for slow communication, saying some travelers learned of cancellations only at the gate. The airline's shares fell 4 percent on Monday.

The state education department released test results showing that average eighth-grade math scores rose by 3 points compared with last year, the first increase since 2018. Reading scores were flat. Officials credited a tutoring program that reached about 40,000 students in low-income districts. Critics noted that scores remain below pre-pandemic levels and that participation in the tutoring program was voluntary, which may make the comparison with non-participants unreliable. The department plans to expand the program next fall if funding is approved.

Wildfire crews in the northern valley reached 55 percent containment on Thursday after five days of fighting a blaze that has burned 31,000 acres. About 1,200 residents remain under evacuation orders, while 3,000 others were allowed to return home. Officials said 14 homes were destroyed and no deaths have been reported. Cooler temperatures and light rain are forecast through the weekend, but fire managers warned that gusty winds on Sunday could push flames toward two small towns. The cause is under investigation.

A major grocery chain announced it will stop selling eggs from caged hens by 2028, joining several competitors that have made similar pledges. The company said the move would raise egg prices by about 8 percent in the short term. Animal welfare groups welcomed the decision but noted that previous industry pledges have been delayed or abandoned. Egg producers said they will need roughly $2 billion in industry-wide investment to convert barns, and that supply could tighten during the transition.

Scientists using a space telescope have detected water vapor in the atmosphere of a planet about 120 light-years from Earth. The planet, roughly twice the size of Earth, orbits within the habitable zone of its star, where temperatures could allow liquid water. The researchers cautioned that the planet may be a mini-Neptune with a thick hydrogen atmosphere rather than a rocky world, and that detecting water vapor does not mean the planet is habitable. Follow-up observations are planned for next year to measure the atmosphere's composition more precisely.

A local library system will end late fees permanently starting next month, after a pilot program showed that eliminating fines did not reduce the number of returned books. The pilot, run at six branches over a year, found that returns were on time 87 percent of the time compared with 85 percent before. Library officials said fines disproportionately kept low-income families from borrowing. The change will cost the system about $300,000 a year in lost revenue, which the county has agreed to cover. Patrons will still be charged for books that are lost or damaged.

The county health board announced that a mobile clinic will begin visiting six rural towns every other week starting in April, offering vaccinations, blood pressure checks and basic dental screenings at no charge. The program is funded by a $1.2 million state grant and staffed by two nurses, a dentist and a driver. Board members said some residents currently drive more than an hour to reach the nearest clinic. One commissioner questioned whether the grant would last beyond its two-year term, and the board said it will seek local funding if the program proves popular.

A technology company said on Wednesday that it will lay off about 900 employees, roughly 7 percent of its workforce, as it shifts spending toward artificial intelligence products. The chief executive said in a memo that affected workers will receive 16 weeks of severance and extended health coverage. The company reported a 12 percent rise in quarterly revenue but a smaller profit than analysts expected. Its shares rose 2 percent in after-hours trading. A labor group said the cuts show that strong revenue no longer protects jobs.
